catalog_quote: [Schuh 1978 p. 65] 7.1.2. Tone classes. Monosyllabic verbs all have high tone; CVVC- and CVCC- all have low tone; for CVC- roots there is a lexical distinction between high and low tone roots. Although the high tone type is almost three times as common (32 out of 43 CVC- roots collected), there is no way to predict the tone class of a CVC-verb. In fact one minimal pair was found (see 'give' and 'return' below). [p. 9] These languages all have two phonemic tones only. [Schuh 2017 p. 6] - stress: no Chadic language has stress as a prosodic parameter [p. 89] All Chadic languages are tone languages, i.e. relative voice pitch on individual syllables is part of the lexical representation of words and has the potential for making morphosyntactic distinctions. ... Stress as distinctive prosodic property has been discussed in Hunter (1980) for Hausa and Wolff (1983, 2015b) for Lamang (and perhaps in a few other Chadic language studies), but prosodic amplitude in Chadic phonological systems generally is a function of the interaction of tone, syllable weight, and intonation and plays no role that is not attributable to those properties.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Per Schuh (who himself produced the only phonological sketch of Galambu, 1978), every Chadic language, hence Galambu, is a lexical/grammatical tone language and none has word stress as an independent prosodic parameter; perceived prominence follows from tone, syllable weight and intonation.
new_statements.exceptions: Schuh notes that stress 'as distinctive prosodic property' has been argued for Hausa (Hunter 1980) and Lamang (Wolff 1983, 2015b) but rejects an independent role for it; no Bole-Tangale exceptions named.
new_statements.domain_note: FAMILY-LEVEL generalization over all Chadic languages, not a Galambu-specific description; Galambu is only named in the book's Bole-Tangale language list. The Galambu-specific phonological sketch is in Schuh 1978 (print only, not seen). Word-level prosody; no discussion of citation forms or phrase-level prominence for Galambu.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is a family-level generalization over all Chadic languages by R. G. Schuh (A Chadic Cornucopia, 2017), not a description of Galambu (gala1264) itself; Schuh is also the author of the only Galambu-specific phonological sketch (1978, print only, not seen). Decker et al. 2022 call the language Galambi and sampled the Pada and Yelwa varieties. If the catalog requires a language-specific statement, treat this entry as provisional pending Schuh 1978.

tone_statements.citation: Schuh, Russell G. 1977. West Chadic verb classes. In Paul Newman & Roxana Ma Newman (eds.), Papers in Chadic Linguistics: Papers from the Leiden Colloquium on the Chadic Language Family, 143-166. (Research Reports 4.) Leiden: Afrika-Studiecentrum.
tone_statements.quote: Verbs in the Bole group have the reconstructed tone pattern (Lo...) Hi with one important exception: verbs which are reflexes of the reconstructed *CV̀Cú type have initial high tone in all the languages except Karekare.⁹ ... Some languages other than Karekare have a small number of CVCu verbs with initial low tone. In most cases there is evidence that these are of secondary origin, resulting from either reduction of a long vowel or geminate consonants with retention of the original tone, e.g. Gera hàl-mí 'he got wet' (cf. Kirfi àllú-wò), Galambu bày-áalà 'he bought' (cf. Kirfi bàayú-wò).
tone_statements.locator: p. 149 sec. 2.1 'The Bole group' (main text) and footnote 9 as continued on p. 150
tone_statements.summary: Comparative paper on verb tone/vowel classes; Galambu verb tones given only as Hi/Lo patterns (perfective (Lo.)Hi, subjunctive like Kirfi, p.153); no inventory, TBU or downstep statement for Galambu.
